name: Thiruthalinathar Temple, Thiruppathur (Thiruputhur)
deity: Shiva as Thiruthalinathar, with the goddess Sivakami; renowned for its Yoga Bhairavar
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu, sung by Appar and Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); Pandya inscriptions of the 9th century
dynasty: Pandya (Varaguna II records), restored under the later Pandyas; Marudhu brothers' additions
summary: In Thiruppathur near Karaikudi, the Thiruputhur of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped as Thiruthalinathar, beside a rare Bhairava seated in yogic stillness.

sections.history: Thiruppathur is a market town in Sivaganga district, about 20 km from Karaikudi, and its great Shiva temple is the Thiruputhur of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted sixth among the fourteen of Pandya Nadu; both Appar and Sambandar sang its Lord. Two inscriptions of 868 and 878 CE, from the reign of the Pandya king Varaguna II, show the temple flourishing in the ninth century. Damaged in the turbulent fourteenth century, it was repaired and its images reconsecrated by Visalayadevar of Kunrakkudi under the Pandya king Jatavarman Vira Pandya, and in the eighteenth century the Marudhu brothers of Sivaganga added to its halls.
sections.architecture: The temple spreads across a broad site with four enclosures, and its vimana is known for fine stucco work. The most celebrated shrine is that of Yoga Bhairavar in the second enclosure: facing west, Bhairava is seated in the still posture of a yogi rather than standing with his dog — a rare form. The hall before it is attributed to the Marudhu brothers, whose figures are carved there. The outer enclosure holds a shrine of Thirunageswarar, and the temple tanks include the Thali theertham and the Sivagangai.
sections.legends: The sthala purana gives the place two names. Shiva is said to have danced the Gauri Thandavam here, and Mahalakshmi — Thiru — worshipped him after witnessing it, so he became Thiruthalinathar. Earlier still, the sage Valmiki is said to have sat in penance so long that an anthill, a puttru, rose over him, giving the town its name Thiruputhur. The serpents Vasuki and Karkotaka are also said to have worshipped here, remembered at the Thirunageswarar shrine.
sections.festivals: The Yoga Bhairavar shrine draws large numbers on Ashtami days, especially the waning-moon Ashtami sacred to Bhairava, and on Bhairava Ashtami in the month of Karthigai. The Shaiva year — Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri, Arudra Darshanam and the days of the goddess Sivakami — is kept with devotion. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Come for Thiruthalinathar and stay for Bhairava: many pilgrims know this as the Vairavan temple, and the quiet, seated Bhairava is unlike any other in the region. Walk all four enclosures, look for the Marudhu brothers in the Bhairava hall, and combine the visit with Piranmalai and the Chettinad towns close by.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; Ashtami days are busy at the Bhairava shrine. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum or the Bhairava shrine; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruppathur is about 65 km from Madurai, 20–25 km from Karaikudi and about 35 km from Sivaganga, with frequent buses on all three routes. Karaikudi is the nearest major railway station, and Madurai Airport the nearest airport.
